paragraphs.text: וַתֵּצֵ֤א דִינָה֙ בַּת־לֵאָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָלְדָ֖ה לְיַעֲקֹ֑ב לִרְא֖וֹת בִּבְנ֥וֹת הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And Dinah, the daughter of Le'ah, whom she had borne to Ya'aqov, went out to see the daughters of the land.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֨רְא אֹתָ֜הּ שְׁכֶ֧ם בֶּן־חֲמ֛וֹר הַֽחִוִּ֖י נְשִׂ֣יא הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּקַּ֥ח אֹתָ֛הּ וַיִּשְׁכַּ֥ב אֹתָ֖הּ וַיְעַנֶּֽהָ׃

i18n.en: And Shechem the son of Chamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her; and he took her, and lay with her, and humbled her.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-ye'aneha* (וַיְעַנֶּהָ — Piel of *ʿ-n-h* II) is the chapter's foundational philological crux. The verbal chain *va-yiqach otah va-yishkav otah va-ye'aneha* — *and he took her, and lay with her, and \[innah\]'d her* — is read across modern critical scholarship in two principal directions: (i) as climaxing a violence-sequence (rape; so Sternberg 1985, Fewell-Gunn *JBL* 110 [1991], Frymer-Kensky *Reading the Women of the Bible* 1998, Scholz *Rape Plots* 2000; reflected in NJPS *lay with her by force*); (ii) as naming the social-status consequence of the act (lost marriageability) without committing to act-modality (Bechtel *JSOT* 62 [1994] 19-36; Yamada *Configurations of Rape in the Hebrew Bible* 2008; partially HALOT s.v. *ʿ-n-h* II). Cross-corpus the Piel of *ʿ-n-h* II is mixed: Deut 21:14 (post-capture; status); Deut 22:24, 29 (forced sex); Judg 19:24, 20:5 (rape); 2 Sam 13:12, 14, 22, 32 (Amnon and Tamar — rape); Lam 5:11 (rape of the women of Zion); Exod 1:11-12 (oppression without sexual sense). The translation surface preserves ASV *humbled her* — the philologically conservative choice that preserves the lexeme's ambiguity rather than resolving it to a single reading. See the central glossary entry `innah-piel-anah-philological-crux-rape-or-shame` for the full corpus and citations.

The verb *va-yishkav otah* — *lay with her* with the accusative-marker *otah* rather than the customary preposition *imah* (*with her*) or *etah* — is itself read by Sternberg and Alter as a syntactic-marker of coercion: the verb takes the woman as direct-object rather than as the equal partner of a *lying-with*. The reading is not consensus (Wenham regards it as inconclusive) but is widely noted.

paragraphs.text: וַתִּדְבַּ֣ק נַפְשׁ֔וֹ בְּדִינָ֖ה בַּֽת־יַעֲקֹ֑ב וַיֶּֽאֱהַב֙ אֶת־הַֽנַּעֲרָ֔ וַיְדַבֵּ֖ר עַל־לֵ֥ב הַֽנַּעֲרָֽ׃

i18n.en: And his soul clung to Dinah the daughter of Ya'aqov, and he loved the young woman, and spoke to the heart of the young woman.

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse's affect-vocabulary — *va-tidbaq nafsho* (*his soul clung*), *va-ye'ehav* (*he loved*), *va-yedabber al-lev* (*spoke to the heart of*) — contrasts sharply in register with the violence-syntax of v 2. The juxtaposition is one of the chapter's most-noted literary features and is read across modern critical scholarship in two directions: (a) source-critical layering (Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985; Speiser *AB* 1964) — vv 2 and 3 belong to different documentary strands; (b) deliberate narratorial juxtaposition (Sternberg 1985; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004; Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* 1975) — the editor stages the ethical incommensurability of the act with the affect.

The idiom *va-yedabber al-lev* (*spoke upon the heart of*) recurs at Gen 50:21 (Yosef to his brothers), Ruth 2:13 (Bo'az to Rut), Isa 40:2 (the prophet to Yerushalayim), Hos 2:16, and Judg 19:3 — in every instance as tender consoling speech, never coercive. The ASV-baseline *spoke to the heart of the young woman* is preserved literally; NJPS / NRSV smooth to *spoke tenderly to her*.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁכֶ֔ם אֶל־חֲמ֥וֹר אָבִ֖יו לֵאמֹ֑ר קַֽח־לִ֛י אֶת־הַיַּלְדָּ֥ה הַזֹּ֖את לְאִשָּֽׁה׃

i18n.en: And Shechem spoke to Chamor his father, saying, Get me this girl as wife.

paragraphs.text: וְיַעֲקֹ֣ב שָׁמַ֗ע כִּ֤י טִמֵּא֙ אֶת־דִּינָ֣ה בִתּ֔וֹ וּבָנָ֛יו הָי֥וּ אֶת־מִקְנֵ֖הוּ בַּשָּׂדֶ֑ה וְהֶחֱרִ֥שׁ יַעֲקֹ֖ב עַד־בֹּאָֽם׃

i18n.en: Now Ya'aqov heard that he had defiled Dinah his daughter; and his sons were with his cattle in the field: and Ya'aqov held his peace until they came.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Timme* (טִמֵּא — Piel pf 3ms of *t-m-'* I, *to defile / make ritually unclean*) is ritual-purity vocabulary — the same root that governs Lev 11-15 (animal- and bodily-purity legislation) and Lev 18-20 (sexual-defilement legislation). Its deployment at vv 5, 13, 27 is the chapter's foundational classification-move: Dinah's social and ritual status is rendered *defiled*. The verb names a state, not an act-modality; it is consistent with either a rape-reading or a status-degradation reading of v 2 *va-ye'aneha* and does not resolve between them. See the central glossary entry `timme-piel-defilement-language-dinah-shechem` for the cross-corpus distribution and the Klawans / Frymer-Kensky readings.

Ya'aqov's silence (*ve-hecherish Ya'aqov ad bo'am*) is editorially notable. The verb *charash* (to be silent, deaf) recurs at 2 Sam 13:20 (David's silence after Amnon's rape of Tamar) — the only HB parallel of paternal-silence-after-sexual-outrage. The Tamar / Dinah typology is mainstream in modern critical scholarship (Sarna, Alter, Fokkelman).

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּצֵ֛א חֲמ֥וֹר אֲבִֽי־שְׁכֶ֖ם אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹ֑ב לְדַבֵּ֖ר אִתּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Chamor, the father of Shechem, went out to Ya'aqov to speak with him.

paragraphs.text: וּבְנֵ֨י יַעֲקֹ֜ב בָּ֤אוּ מִן־הַשָּׂדֶה֙ כְּשָׁמְעָ֔ם וַיִּֽתְעַצְּבוּ֙ הָֽאֲנָשִׁ֔ים וַיִּ֥חַר לָהֶ֖ם מְאֹ֑ד כִּֽי־נְבָלָ֞ה עָשָׂ֣ה בְיִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל לִשְׁכַּב֙ אֶת־בַּֽת־יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְכֵ֖ן לֹ֥א יֵעָשֶֽׂה׃

i18n.en: And the sons of Ya'aqov came in from the field when they heard it; and the men were grieved, and they were very angry, because he had wrought folly in Yisra'el in lying with Ya'aqov's daughter; for such a thing ought not to be done.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Nevalah* (נְבָלָה) is technical vocabulary for a community-breaching grave offense requiring communal response. The cross-corpus distribution is small and decisive — Deut 22:21 (the case of the falsely-married non-virgin); Judg 19:23-24 + 20:6, 10 (the Gibeah outrage); 2 Sam 13:12 (Tamar's protest to Amnon); Jer 29:23 (false-prophecy and adultery) — clustered without exception at sites of sexual + communal outrage. The foundational philological study is Phillips *VT* 25 (1975) 237-242; see also TDOT IX s.v. *nbl* (Marböck) and HALOT s.v. *nevalah*. The ASV-baseline *folly* is the traditional rendering but under-represents the lexeme's technical force; NJPS / NRSV *outrage* is more accurate. The translation preserves ASV *folly* per the chapter's literal-translation discipline; the technical sense is recorded in the central glossary entry `nevalah-outrage-formula-communal-sexual-offense`.

The phrase *nevalah ... be-Yisra'el* — *outrage in / against Yisra'el* — is grammatically ambiguous at this verse, the formula's earliest HB occurrence. Two readings: (i) personal — *be-Yisra'el* refers to Ya'aqov-as-Yisra'el, the personal name granted at Gen 32:29 / 35:10, and the outrage is against him personally; (ii) collective — *be-Yisra'el* refers to the people-of-Yisra'el, anachronistic at the patriarchal-narrative-level (the people is not yet formed). The collective sense is exclusive elsewhere in the *nevalah be-Yisra'el* formula's later occurrences, and Sarna, Westermann, and Hamilton read the Gen 34:7 occurrence as the formula's editorial first-deployment, activating the collective sense at the cost of patriarchal-period anachronism. The translation preserves ASV *in Yisra'el*; the personal / collective ambiguity is recorded in the central glossary entry `nevalah-be-yisrael-formula-collective-anachronism`.

paragraphs.text: וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר חֲמ֖וֹר אִתָּ֣ם לֵאמֹ֑ר שְׁכֶ֣ם בְּנִ֗י חָֽשְׁקָ֤ה נַפְשׁוֹ֙ בְּבִתְּכֶ֔ם תְּנ֨וּ נָ֥א אֹתָ֛הּ ל֖וֹ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃

i18n.en: And Chamor spoke with them, saying, The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter: I pray you, give her to him as wife.

paragraphs.text: וְהִֽתְחַתְּנ֖וּ אֹתָ֑נוּ בְּנֹֽתֵיכֶם֙ תִּתְּנוּ־לָ֔נוּ וְאֶת־בְּנֹתֵ֖ינוּ תִּקְח֥וּ לָכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And make marriages with us: give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.

paragraphs.text: וְאִתָּ֖נוּ תֵּשֵׁ֑בוּ וְהָאָ֙רֶץ֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה לִפְנֵיכֶ֔ם שְׁבוּ֙ וּסְחָר֔וּהָ וְהֵֽאָחֲז֖וּ בָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And you shall dwell with us: and the land shall be before you; dwell and trade in it, and get possessions in it.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁכֶם֙ אֶל־אָבִ֣יה וְאֶל־אַחֶ֔יהָ אֶמְצָא־חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֵיכֶ֑ם וַאֲשֶׁ֥ר תֹּאמְר֛וּ אֵלַ֖י אֶתֵּֽן׃

i18n.en: And Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you shall say to me I will give.

paragraphs.text: הַרְבּ֨וּ עָלַ֤י מְאֹד֙ מֹ֣הַר וּמַתָּ֔ן וְאֶ֨תְּנָ֔ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר תֹּאמְר֖וּ אֵלָ֑י וּתְנוּ־לִ֥י אֶת־הַֽנַּעֲרָ֖ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃

i18n.en: Ask of me ever so much bride-price and gift, and I will give as you shall say to me: only give me the young woman as wife.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Mohar* (מֹהַר — *bride-price*) is rare: only three HB occurrences. Gen 34:12 (here); Exod 22:16 (the legal-text for the unbetrothed-virgin — *mahor yimhrennah lo l'ishah*); 1 Sam 18:25 (Shaul's request of one hundred Philistine foreskins as *mohar* for Mikhal). The lexeme names a defined legal-payment from the groom to the bride's father at the marriage-contract's establishment — distinct from a dowry (bride-to-groom) and from a gift (free-of-legal-stipulation). The ANE comparative material (Middle Assyrian Laws §§55-56; Code of Hammurabi §§159-161; Nuzi marriage-contracts; cf. Pritchard *ANET*) supports the *mohar* as a defined institutional payment.

ASV's *dowry* is technically misleading (a dowry flows in the opposite direction); NJPS / NRSV / NIV *bride-price* and *marriage present* are more accurate. The WoH translation adopts *bride-price* — a divergence from ASV-baseline justified by lexical precision. See the central glossary entry `mohar-bride-price-three-verse-corpus` for the corpus and the comparative ANE legal-text material.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעֲנ֨וּ בְנֵֽי־יַעֲקֹ֜ב אֶת־שְׁכֶ֨ם וְאֶת־חֲמ֥וֹר אָבִ֛יו בְּמִרְמָ֖ה וַיְדַבֵּ֑רוּ אֲשֶׁ֣ר טִמֵּ֔א אֵ֖ת דִּינָ֥ה אֲחֹתָֽם׃

i18n.en: And the sons of Ya'aqov answered Shechem and Chamor his father with deceit, and spoke, because he had defiled Dinah their sister.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Be-mirmah* (בְּמִרְמָה — *with deceit / deception*) is an explicit narrator-framing of the brothers' speech as deceptive. The exact prepositional phrase recurs only at Gen 27:35 and Gen 34:13 in the Genesis narrative-prose, and once more at 2 Kgs 9:23 (Yehoram's word to Achazyah: *mirmah Achazyahu* — *treachery, Achazyahu!*). The Gen 27:35 → Gen 34:13 lexical echo is one of the most-cited cross-references in modern critical scholarship: Yitzchaq's words to Esav — *ba achikha b-mirmah va-yiqach birkhatekha* (*your brother came with deceit and has taken your blessing*) — are reactivated here in the narrator's own voice as the sons of Ya'aqov reproduce their father's deceptive-pattern against the Shechemites. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 234, Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 187-188, and Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* 1975 pp. 224-225 read the echo as editorially deliberate: Ya'aqov's own *aqav*-character (Gen 25:26, 27:36, 29:25, 30:37-43, 31:20, 33:14) reaches its inheritance moment in his sons' speech. See the central glossary entry `be-mirmah-deception-ya-aqov-cycle-inheritance` for the full cross-reference.

The ASV-baseline *with guile* is preserved as the WoH choice *with deceit* — slightly modernized but lexically equivalent. The translation does not commit to whether the *be-mirmah* belongs grammatically to the brothers' answer (as I render it: *answered ... with deceit*) or to the act itself (*answered ... and spoke deceptively because*); the MT cantillation supports the former.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֲלֵיהֶ֗ם לֹ֤א נוּכַל֙ לַעֲשׂוֹת֙ הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה לָתֵת֙ אֶת־אֲחֹתֵ֔נוּ לְאִ֖ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־ל֣וֹ עָרְלָ֑ה כִּֽי־חֶרְפָּ֥ה הִ֖וא לָֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: And they said to them, We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one that is uncircumcised; for that would be a reproach to us.

paragraphs.text: אַךְ־בְּזֹ֖את נֵא֣וֹת לָכֶ֑ם אִ֚ם תִּהְי֣וּ כָמֹ֔נוּ לְהִמֹּ֥ל לָכֶ֖ם כָּל־זָכָֽר׃

i18n.en: Only on this condition will we consent to you: if you will be as we are, that every male of you be circumcised;

paragraphs.text: וְנָתַ֤נּוּ אֶת־בְּנֹתֵ֙ינוּ֙ לָכֶ֔ם וְאֶת־בְּנֹתֵיכֶ֖ם נִֽקַּֽח־לָ֑נוּ וְיָשַׁ֣בְנוּ אִתְּכֶ֔ם וְהָיִ֖ינוּ לְעַ֥ם אֶחָֽד׃

i18n.en: Then will we give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters to us, and we will dwell with you, and we will become one people.

paragraphs.text: וְאִם־לֹ֧א תִשְׁמְע֛וּ אֵלֵ֖ינוּ לְהִמּ֑וֹל וְלָקַ֥חְנוּ אֶת־בִּתֵּ֖נוּ וְהָלָֽכְנוּ׃

i18n.en: But if you will not listen to us, to be circumcised; then will we take our daughter, and we will be gone.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּֽיטְב֥וּ דִבְרֵיהֶ֖ם בְּעֵינֵ֣י חֲמ֑וֹר וּבְעֵינֵ֖י שְׁכֶ֥ם בֶּן־חֲמֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: And their words were good in the eyes of Chamor, and in the eyes of Shechem the son of Chamor.

paragraphs.text: וְלֹֽא־אֵחַ֤ר הַנַּ֙עַר֙ לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת הַדָּבָ֔ר כִּ֥י חָפֵ֖ץ בְּבַֽת־יַעֲקֹ֑ב וְה֣וּא נִכְבָּ֔ד מִכֹּ֖ל בֵּ֥ית אָבִֽיו׃

i18n.en: And the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he had delight in Ya'aqov's daughter: and he was honored above all the house of his father.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֥א חֲמ֛וֹר וּשְׁכֶ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ אֶל־שַׁ֣עַר עִירָ֑ם וַֽיְדַבְּר֛וּ אֶל־אַנְשֵׁ֥י עִירָ֖ם לֵאמֹֽר׃

i18n.en: And Chamor and Shechem his son came to the gate of their city, and spoke with the men of their city, saying,

paragraphs.commentary:
*Sha'ar ha-ir* (שַׁעַר הָעִיר — *the gate of the city*) is the HB's principal legal-civic-forum setting. The cross-corpus distribution is dense: Gen 19:1 (Lot at the gate of Sedom, judicial role); Gen 23:10, 18 (Avraham's Makhpelah-purchase at the gate of Hevron — see the central entry `patriarchal-land-acquisition-pattern-makhpelah-shechem`); Deut 21:19, 22:15, 25:7 (the elders-at-the-gate legal-formulae for capital cases, contested-virginity, levirate-refusal); Josh 20:4 (the cities-of-refuge legal-formula); Ruth 4:1, 11 (Bo'az's redemption-transaction at the gate of Beit-Lechem); 2 Sam 15:2 (Avshalom's gate-of-the-city intercepting of litigants); etc. The motif is one of the HB's foundational legal-procedural-settings.

The Gen 23 / Gen 34 parallel is editorially significant: both patriarchal narratives stage a city-gate negotiation between the Ya'aqov / Avraham family and a named-local-Canaanite population (the *bnei Het* at Hevron in Gen 23; the *bnei Chamor* at Shechem in Gen 34), but the Gen 34 negotiation is *be-mirmah* (v 13) — the legal-civic-forum is exploited as the deception's framework. See the central glossary entry `sha-ar-ha-ir-city-gate-legal-civic-assembly` for the cross-corpus material.

paragraphs.text: הָאֲנָשִׁ֨ים הָאֵ֜לֶּה שְֽׁלֵמִ֧ים הֵ֣ם אִתָּ֗נוּ וְיֵשְׁב֤וּ בָאָ֙רֶץ֙ וְיִסְחֲר֣וּ אֹתָ֔הּ וְהָאָ֛רֶץ הִנֵּ֥ה רַֽחֲבַת־יָדַ֖יִם לִפְנֵיהֶ֑ם אֶת־בְּנֹתָם֙ נִקַּֽח־לָ֣נוּ לְנָשִׁ֔ים וְאֶת־בְּנֹתֵ֖ינוּ נִתֵּ֥ן לָהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: These men are peaceable with us; therefore let them dwell in the land, and trade in it; for, behold, the land is large enough for them; let us take their daughters to us as wives, and let us give them our daughters.

paragraphs.text: אַךְ־בְּ֠זֹאת יֵאֹ֨תוּ לָ֤נוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים֙ לָשֶׁ֣בֶת אִתָּ֔נוּ לִהְי֖וֹת לְעַ֣ם אֶחָ֑ד בְּהִמּ֥וֹל לָ֙נוּ֙ כָּל־זָכָ֔ר כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר הֵ֥ם נִמֹּלִֽים׃

i18n.en: Only on this condition will the men consent to us to dwell with us, to become one people, that every male among us be circumcised, as they are circumcised.

paragraphs.text: מִקְנֵהֶ֤ם וְקִנְיָנָם֙ וְכָל־בְּהֶמְתָּ֔ם הֲל֥וֹא לָ֖נוּ הֵ֑ם אַ֚ךְ נֵא֣וֹתָה לָהֶ֔ם וְיֵשְׁב֖וּ אִתָּֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: Shall not their cattle and their substance and all their beasts be ours? only let us consent to them, and they will dwell with us.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁמְע֤וּ אֶל־חֲמוֹר֙ וְאֶל־שְׁכֶ֣ם בְּנ֔וֹ כָּל־יֹצְאֵ֖י שַׁ֣עַר עִיר֑וֹ וַיִּמֹּ֙לוּ֙ כָּל־זָכָ֔ר כָּל־יֹצְאֵ֖י שַׁ֥עַר עִירֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And all that went out of the gate of his city listened to Chamor and to Shechem his son; and every male was circumcised, all that went out of the gate of his city.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִי֩ בַיּ֨וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֜י בִּֽהְיוֹתָ֣ם כֹּֽאֲבִ֗ים וַיִּקְח֣וּ שְׁנֵֽי־בְנֵי־יַ֠עֲקֹב שִׁמְע֨וֹן וְלֵוִ֜י אֲחֵ֤י דִינָה֙ אִ֣ישׁ חַרְבּ֔וֹ וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ עַל־הָעִ֖יר בֶּ֑טַח וַיַּֽהַרְג֖וּ כָּל־זָכָֽר׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass on the third day, when they were in pain, that two of the sons of Ya'aqov, Shim'on and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took each man his sword, and came upon the city unawares, and killed every male.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ba-yom ha-shlishi* (בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי — *on the third day*) is the chapter's deployment of the HB stylized third-day formula. The formula marks theophany, decisive event, or transition across the canon (Gen 22:4 *aqedah*; Gen 31:22 Lavan's pursuit; Gen 40:20 Pharaoh's birthday; Gen 42:18 Yosef releases the brothers; Exod 19:11, 15-16 Sinai theophany; Hos 6:2 prophetic resurrection-formula; etc.). The Gen 34:25 occurrence specifically pairs the third-day with *bi-hyotam ko'avim* (*when they were in pain*) — the surgical-recovery-pain peak of male circumcision (cf. Josh 5:8 *ad chayotam* — *until they were healed* — of the wilderness-circumcision generation, where the recovery is multi-day). See the central glossary entry `ba-yom-ha-shlishi-third-day-formula` for the full cross-corpus distribution.

*Betach* (בֶּטַח — *securely / confidently / unawares*) is lexically ambiguous between two referential targets: (i) the city's-state reading — the city was unsuspecting / unaware (so ASV *unawares*, NIV *unsuspecting*, Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 235, Hamilton *NICOT* 1995 p. 367); (ii) the attackers'-state reading — the brothers came confidently / boldly (so NJPS *confidently*, Targum Onqelos, Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 p. 539). The lexeme elsewhere admits both readings (Lev 25:18-19; 26:5; Deut 12:10; Judg 18:7, 27 — *am shoket u-voteach* of the unsuspecting Laish-citizens, a strong city's-state parallel to Gen 34:25). The chapter-narrative-context (the city is in surgical-recovery-pain, deceived) favors the city's-state reading. The translation preserves ASV-baseline *unawares*; the philological alternative is recorded in the overlay entry `betach-shechem-attackers-confident-or-victims-unaware`.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־חֲמוֹר֙ וְאֶת־שְׁכֶ֣ם בְּנ֔וֹ הָרְג֖וּ לְפִי־חָ֑רֶב וַיִּקְח֧וּ אֶת־דִּינָ֛ה מִבֵּ֥ית שְׁכֶ֖ם וַיֵּצֵֽאוּ׃

i18n.en: And they killed Chamor and Shechem his son at the edge of the sword, and took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and went out.

paragraphs.text: בְּנֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֗ב בָּ֚אוּ עַל־הַ֣חֲלָלִ֔ים וַיָּבֹ֖זּוּ הָעִ֑יר אֲשֶׁ֥ר טִמְּא֖וּ אֲחוֹתָֽם׃

i18n.en: The sons of Ya'aqov came upon the slain, and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister.

paragraphs.commentary:
The grammatical-subject shifts from *Shim'on and Levi* (vv 25-26, two named brothers acting alone with their swords) to *bnei Ya'aqov* (the collective *sons of Ya'aqov*, here and at v 27 onward). Modern critical scholarship reads this as a documentary-source seam (so Speiser *AB* 1964 pp. 264-266; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 535-540; Hamilton *NICOT* 1995 pp. 366-368): vv 25-26 represent an older two-brothers-alone-slaughter tradition; v 27 onward represents a later collective-plundering layer harmonized to it. The narrative-critical alternative (Sternberg, Sarna) reads the shift as deliberate: Shim'on and Levi do the killing; the wider brotherhood plunders the aftermath. The translation preserves the MT surface without committing.

The verb of v 27's relative-clause — *asher timm'u achotam* (*because they had defiled their sister*) — is the chapter's third deployment of *timme* (cf. vv 5, 13). The grammatical-subject is plural (*they had defiled*), broadening the defilement-frame from Shechem alone (v 5) to a collective Shechemite responsibility. The shift is the chapter's most explicit rhetorical move toward collective-Shechemite culpability.

paragraphs.text: אֶת־צֹאנָ֥ם וְאֶת־בְּקָרָ֖ם וְאֶת־חֲמֹרֵיהֶ֑ם וְאֵ֧ת אֲשֶׁר־בָּעִ֛יר וְאֶת־אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּשָּׂדֶ֖ה לָקָֽחוּ׃

i18n.en: They took their flocks and their herds and their donkeys, and that which was in the city, and that which was in the field;

paragraphs.commentary: The plunder-list across vv 28-29 (*tzonam u-vqaram va-chamoreihem ... chelam ... tapam u-nsheihem shavu va-yavozu*) follows the stylized HB warfare-plunder-formula: flocks-and-herds-and-donkeys + city-contents + field-contents + wealth + little-ones-and-wives-as-captives. The form parallels Num 31:9-11 (the Midianite-war), Josh 8:2 (the Ai-capture), Deut 20:14 (the foreign-city-of-war legal-formula), and 1 Sam 15:3 (the Amaleq-war). Modern critical scholarship (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 236; Sternberg 1985; Brenner *I Am: Biblical Women Tell Their Own Stories* 2005) reads the formula's deployment here as a proto-*cherem*-warfare narrative, marking the slaughter as anomalous within the patriarchal narrative-frame (which does not elsewhere stage holy-war-plunder). The translation does not commit to the proto-*cherem* reading; the formula-recognition is recorded in commentary only.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־כָּל־חֵילָ֤ם וְאֶת־כָּל־טַפָּם֙ וְאֶת־נְשֵׁיהֶ֔ם שָׁב֖וּ וַיָּבֹ֑זּוּ וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּבָּֽיִת׃

i18n.en: and all their wealth, and all their little ones and their wives, they took captive and plundered, even all that was in the house.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֜ב אֶל־שִׁמְע֣וֹן וְאֶל־לֵוִי֮ עֲכַרְתֶּ֣ם אֹתִי֒ לְהַבְאִישֵׁ֙נִי֙ בְּיֹשֵׁ֣ב הָאָ֔רֶץ בַּֽכְּנַעֲנִ֖י וּבַפְּרִזִּ֑י וַאֲנִי֙ מְתֵ֣י מִסְפָּ֔ר וְנֶאֶסְפ֤וּ עָלַי֙ וְהִכּ֔וּנִי וְנִשְׁמַדְתִּ֖י אֲנִ֥י וּבֵיתִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said to Shim'on and Levi, You have troubled me, to make me odious to the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanite and the Perizzite: and, I being few in number, they will gather themselves together against me and strike me, and I shall be destroyed, I and my house.

paragraphs.commentary:
Ya'aqov's rebuke is pragmatic, not moral: *akhartem oti l-hav'isheni b-yoshev ha-aretz* — *you have troubled me, to make me stink among the inhabitants of the land*. The verb *akhar* (cf. Josh 7:25 — *akhar Akhan* the troubler-of-Israel at Ai; Judg 11:35 — Yiftach to his daughter) names disruption of political-or-social standing. *Hav'isheni* (literally *to cause-me-to-stink*) is the strongest possible HB idiom for reputational damage (cf. Exod 5:21 — *hiv'ashtem et-reichenu b-eynei Phar'oh*; 1 Sam 13:4; 27:12). Ya'aqov complains of consequences, not of ethics — the chapter's signature dialogic irresolution.

The *ba-Kena'ani u-va-Prizi* doubling (*among the Canaanite and the Perizzite*) re-deploys the redactional formula attested at Gen 12:6 / 13:7. The existing central entry `kenaani-prizi-az-ba-aretz` documents the formula's redactional-vantage; this verse is a character-speech rather than a narrator-parenthetical, and the application is therefore a character-speech extension of the doubling-formula. The translation preserves ASV-baseline *Canaanite and Perizzite* (gentilic-rendering rather than transliteration register).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֑וּ הַכְזוֹנָ֕ה יַעֲשֶׂ֖ה אֶת־אֲחוֹתֵֽנוּ׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And they said, Should he deal with our sister as with a prostitute?

paragraphs.commentary:
The chapter closes on an unanswered rhetorical question: *ha-khe-zonah ya'aseh et-achotenu* — *should he deal with our sister as with a prostitute?* Modern critical scholarship reads the closure as deliberate narratological aporia (Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 445-475; Fewell-Gunn *JBL* 110 [1991] 193-211; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 189-190; Fishbane *Text and Texture* 1979). The chapter ends on the dialogic non-resolution between Ya'aqov's pragmatic-political voice (v 30) and the sons' honor-based voice (v 31); the narrator gives neither party the last word in his own voice.

*Zonah* (זוֹנָה — Qal active participle of *z-n-h*) is pejorative HB status-vocabulary for unsanctioned-sexual-status, widely distributed across the canon: Gen 38:15 (Tamar disguised); Lev 21:7, 14 (priestly marriage-restrictions); Deut 23:18-19; Josh 2:1, 6:17-25 (Rahav); Judg 11:1 (Yiftach's mother); Judg 16:1 (Shimshon at Gaza); 1 Kgs 3:16; Prov 6:26, 7:10, 23:27, 29:3; Isa 1:21, 23:15-16, 57:3; Jer 3:3, 5:7; Ezek 16:30-35, 23:44; Hos 1:2, 2:7, 3:3, 4:14-15; Joel 4:3; Amos 7:17; Mic 1:7; Nah 3:4. ASV-baseline *harlot* preserves the lexeme; NJPS / NRSV *prostitute* is the modern critical equivalent. The WoH adopts *prostitute*. See the central glossary entry `zonah-prostitute-status-vocabulary-cross-corpus` for the cross-corpus material.

The chapter's seeming-vindication-of-the-brothers is pre-empted by Gen 49:5-7 — Ya'aqov's deathbed-curse against Shim'on and Levi for this very slaughter: *Shim'on v-Levi achim klei chamas mekhroteihem ... arur apam ki az v-evratam ki qashatah* — *Shim'on and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords ... cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel*. The retrospective curse is editorially essential: the patriarch's death-bed verdict closes the canonical frame against the sons' honor-claim. The cross-reference is recorded in the overlay entry `ha-khe-zonah-chapter-closing-aporia`.
